title: BEFORE YOU TAKE COMMUNION, THERE IS SOMETHING YOU MUST NOT IGNORE
paragraphs: BEFORE YOU TAKE COMMUNION, THERE IS SOMETHING YOU MUST NOT IGNORE
The terrifying warning of 1 Corinthians 11, the hidden sins we bring to the Lord’s Table, and the breathtaking grace of Jesus Christ that changes everything.
There is a moment in church that can reveal more about your spiritual life than an entire hour of singing.
The pastor lifts the bread.
The cup is prepared.
The congregation grows quiet.
And suddenly, while everyone around you seems ready to receive Communion, something begins stirring inside your heart.
A memory.
A secret.
A conversation you wish you could take back.
A temptation you surrendered to last night.
A sin you promised God you would never commit again.
And then comes the question you are almost afraid to ask.
“Should I even be taking Communion right now?”
You look around.
The woman beside you is praying. The man in front of you has his eyes closed. Someone across the aisle is quietly wiping away tears.
And there you are.
Holding a little piece of bread, wondering whether God sees everything you have been hiding.
He does.
But what happens next may not be what you think.
Because the Bible contains a warning about Communion so serious that the apostle Paul connected its abuse with judgment, weakness, sickness, and even death.

Yet the same Gospel tells us that the blood of Jesus cleanses sinners, that broken people can approach God's throne of grace, and that our hope rests not in our perfection but in Christ's finished work.
How can both be true?
How can the Lord's Table be a place of solemn warning and extraordinary mercy?
And perhaps the most personal question of all:
Must you confess your sins before taking Communion, or can you come to Jesus exactly as you are?
Stay with this question.
Because the answer is not simply about what you do before receiving the bread and cup.
It is about what you believe the blood of Jesus can actually accomplish.
Imagine a man sitting near the back of a church.
He loves Jesus. At least, he believes he does.
But his marriage is strained. His temper has wounded his children. His private life contains compromises nobody in the congregation knows about.
That morning, he argued with his wife before leaving home.
He said something cruel.
He knew it was cruel.
And rather than apologizing, he walked out the door, opened his Bible at church, and began singing about the goodness of God.
Now the Communion elements are being distributed.
His hands reach forward.
But his conscience will not let him forget what happened at home.
Should he take the bread?
Should he drink the cup?
Should he confess first?
Or should he refuse Communion because he knows he has sinned?
To answer that faithfully, we must return to Scripture, not merely to church tradition, personal feelings, or the fear of appearing unspiritual.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 11:27–28:
Read those final words again.
“And so let him eat.”
Paul did not simply say, “Examine yourself and stay away.”
He commanded self-examination and then directed believers toward participation.
That distinction matters enormously.
In the original Greek, the word translated “unworthily” in verse 27 is ἀναξίως (anaxiōs).
It describes an unworthy manner of participating.
It does not mean that only morally flawless people may receive Communion.
If personal sinlessness were the requirement, who among us could approach?
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
The apostle's concern was not that ordinary Christians had suddenly become unworthy of Christ's sacrifice because they still struggled with sin.
His concern was that believers were treating the Lord's Supper in a manner that contradicted the very Gospel it proclaimed.
And the historical context makes that warning even more disturbing.
The church in Corinth was not simply having a private spiritual problem.
They were humiliating one another at the Lord's Table.
Some ate abundantly while others went hungry. Some were drunk while others had nothing. Social divisions were being carried into a sacred gathering meant to proclaim their unity in Christ.
Paul confronted them directly.
In 1 Corinthians 11:21, he wrote:
“For in eating every one taketh before other his own supper: and one is hungry, and another is drunken.”
Think about the contradiction.
They were remembering a Savior who gave Himself for others while refusing to care for the people sitting beside them.
They were proclaiming sacrificial love while practicing selfishness.
They were celebrating the body of Christ while despising members of His church.
That is why Paul refused to treat their behavior as a minor religious mistake.
Communion was never intended to become a performance in which people could appear holy while deliberately disregarding the Lord they claimed to honor.
And that truth reaches far beyond ancient Corinth.
What good is it to speak reverently about the broken body of Jesus while refusing to acknowledge the people our own words have broken?
What does it mean to celebrate the blood that purchased forgiveness while deliberately nurturing bitterness?
How can we proclaim that Christ gave Himself for His people while treating fellow believers as though they do not matter?
These questions should make us uncomfortable.
Not because God delights in humiliating us.
But because genuine grace does not teach us to make peace with the sins from which Jesus came to redeem us.
Paul continues in 1 Corinthians 11:29:
“For he that eateth and drinketh unworthily, eateth and drinketh damnation to himself, not discerning the Lord's body.” (KJV)
The word translated “damnation” is κρίμα (krima), meaning judgment.
In this context, it should not automatically be understood as eternal condemnation.
Paul explains in verse 32 that the Lord's discipline is intended to distinguish His people from the condemnation of the world.
That does not make the warning harmless.
It makes it deeply serious.
Paul even states in verse 30:
“For this cause many are weak and sickly among you, and many sleep.”
The passage presents divine judgment as a real consequence of the Corinthians' irreverent conduct.
We must not explain away Paul's words.
But neither should we misuse them.
This text does not authorize us to tell every sick Christian that their illness is punishment for taking Communion improperly.
Scripture itself rejects the assumption that all suffering can be traced to a particular personal sin.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus corrected His disciples when they attempted to explain a man's blindness through that kind of reasoning.
The warning in Corinth is real.
The context is specific.
And faithful interpretation must honor both.
Now we come to the question that may be weighing on your heart.
Should Christians confess their sins before taking Communion?
Yes. Confession, repentance, and honest self-examination are deeply appropriate responses as believers prepare to remember the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
But we must be precise about what Scripture commands.

First Corinthians 11 explicitly commands believers to examine themselves. It does not prescribe a universal ritual requiring every individual sin to be verbally listed before every celebration of Communion.
Nor does it teach that a Christian must achieve complete moral perfection before participating.
Confession is not a payment that makes the bread and cup safe.
Repentance is not a spiritual fee that purchases access to God's mercy.
And Communion is not a reward handed to Christians who managed to avoid temptation throughout the week.
We confess because God is holy, because sin is serious, because fellowship with Him matters, and because His mercy gives us the courage to stop hiding.
Listen to 1 John 1:9:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
The Greek word translated “confess” is ὁμολογῶμεν (homologōmen), from ὁμολογέω (homologeō).
Its sense is to acknowledge or confess.
In this verse, the idea is not that we inform God about something He does not know.
It is that we honestly acknowledge our sins before Him rather than denying them or pretending they are insignificant.
And notice what John says about God's response.
He is faithful.
He is just.
He forgives.
He cleanses.
How can forgiveness be just when sin deserves judgment?
Because the Christian's confidence rests upon Jesus Christ, whose atoning sacrifice John emphasizes in the surrounding passage.
First John 2:1–2 directs sinning believers to Jesus Christ the righteous, our Advocate with the Father, and identifies Him as the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The believer does not approach God carrying a self-made certificate of innocence.
The believer approaches through the Savior who has dealt with sin at the cross.
That is the difference between Gospel repentance and religious self-punishment.
One looks to Jesus.
The other becomes consumed with the self.
One admits, “Lord, I have sinned, and I need Your mercy.”
The other whispers, “Perhaps if I feel guilty long enough, I will finally deserve Your mercy.”
But guilt cannot accomplish what only Christ's blood can accomplish.
Consider the Greek word δοκιμαζέτω (dokimazetō) in 1 Corinthians 11:28.
It comes from δοκιμάζω (dokimazō), meaning to test, examine, or assess.
Paul's command calls for meaningful self-examination.
Not a frantic search for absolute moral flawlessness.
Not endless anxiety over whether you remembered every sinful thought.
Not an attempt to earn God's acceptance by producing the perfect emotional response.
It is an invitation to examine your conduct and attitude honestly in light of the Lord whose death you are proclaiming.
Are you treating the sacrifice of Christ with reverence?
Are you harboring contempt toward fellow believers?
Are you knowingly defending sin rather than turning from it?
Are you willing to acknowledge your wrongdoing?
Are you approaching the Lord's Table with faith in Christ rather than confidence in your own righteousness?
Those questions matter.
Because there is a difference between a Christian who hates a sin but continues struggling against it and a person who proudly insists that God has no right to challenge their behavior.
There is a difference between stumbling and celebrating the fall.
There is a difference between a wounded conscience crying for mercy and a hardened heart demanding permission to remain unchanged.
Both need Jesus.
But Scripture never presents repentance as optional for someone who wants to follow Him.
Remember the man sitting at the back of the church?
The one who wounded his wife with his words?
Suppose he closes his eyes and prays:

“Lord Jesus, I have sinned. I spoke cruelly to someone You have called me to love. I cannot justify what I said. Please forgive me. Change my heart. Give me the humility to apologize and the grace to live differently.”
That prayer does not magically erase the consequences of his behavior.
His wife may still be hurting.
Trust may need rebuilding.
His repentance must become visible in his actions.
But something important has happened.
He has stopped defending his sin.
He has brought it into the light.
And he is looking to Christ for mercy and transformation.
After Communion, he still needs to go home, apologize sincerely, and pursue reconciliation.

Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:23–24 underscores the seriousness of reconciliation when someone has something against us. Although that passage concerns bringing a gift to the altar rather than specifically receiving Communion, its principle challenges any attempt to separate worship from responsibility toward others.
We cannot claim to honor Christ's sacrifice while treating repentance as an inconvenience.
Yet we must also avoid another dangerous mistake.
Some Christians believe that the more deeply they feel ashamed, the more acceptable their confession becomes.
They imagine that God is waiting for them to produce enough tears.
Enough sorrow.
Enough emotional pain.
As though forgiveness begins only after they have suffered sufficiently for what they have done.
But Scripture does not teach that your emotional intensity purchases forgiveness.
Psalm 51:17 declares:
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.”
In the Hebrew text, the phrase לֵב־נִשְׁבָּר וְנִדְכֶּה (lev-nishbar ve-nidkeh) describes a broken and crushed or contrite heart.
David's words arose from the terrible reality of his own sin.
He had committed adultery.
He had arranged the death of Uriah.
He had attempted to conceal what he had done.
Yet when confronted, David could not save himself through religious performance.
He needed mercy.
And his confession in Psalm 51 was not an excuse to continue sinning.
It was the cry of a man who understood that he had sinned against a holy God.
That is the heart of repentance.
Not pretending the sin was small.
Not pretending the sinner was beyond redemption.
But agreeing with God's judgment about sin while appealing to God's mercy.
And here is where the beauty of the Gospel becomes almost overwhelming.
On the night Jesus instituted the Lord's Supper, He was surrounded by disciples who were far from perfect.
Peter would deny Him.
The others would flee.
Judas would betray Him.
Jesus knew the darkness that was about to unfold.
And still, He willingly went to the cross.
In Luke 22:19, Jesus said:
“This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me.”
Those words should stop us.
“Given for you.”
Not because humanity had finally become righteous enough.
Not because His disciples had proven themselves incapable of failure.
Not because the world deserved the sacrifice.
But because the Son of God came to accomplish what sinners could never accomplish for themselves.
And when Jesus spoke of the cup, He connected it to the new covenant in His blood.
In Matthew 26:28, He declared:
“For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.”
The word translated “remission” is ἄφεσιν (aphesin), from ἄφεσις (aphesis), meaning forgiveness or release.
The cup points to the forgiveness made possible through Christ's sacrificial death.
It is not an invitation to trivialize sin.
It is a proclamation of how costly forgiveness truly is.
The cross tells us that our sins are too serious to dismiss.
And that God's love is too great to measure by our failures.
That is why Communion should produce both reverence and gratitude.
We remember the suffering of Christ.
We proclaim His death.
We acknowledge our need for mercy.
And we look forward to His return.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 11:26:
Communion looks backward to Calvary and forward to the return of Jesus.
It calls us to remember what He has done and to live in anticipation of the day when faith becomes sight.
This is not an ordinary meal.
But neither is it a ceremony designed to drive every struggling believer into despair.
Think about Peter.
A man who promised loyalty.
A man who insisted he would stand with Jesus even if others abandoned Him.
And then, under pressure, he denied knowing his Lord.
Three times.
Imagine the shame.
The memory of his own voice.
The realization that the One he loved had been rejected by his own lips.
Luke 22:61–62 records that Jesus looked at Peter and that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
Yet Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility to care for His sheep, as recorded in John 21:15–19.
Jesus did not pretend Peter's denial had never happened.
He addressed Peter personally.
He restored him graciously.
And He called him forward.
Not because betrayal became harmless.
Not because sin suddenly ceased to matter.
But because Jesus Christ is greater than the failures of those who return to Him in repentance and faith.
Perhaps that is the part of this message you needed to hear.
You have been avoiding Communion because you remember what you did.
Or perhaps you have been taking Communion while refusing to confront what you are still doing.
Those are different spiritual conditions.
And both require honest attention.
If you are avoiding the Lord's Table because you believe Jesus cannot forgive a repentant sinner like you, remember the promise of 1 John 1:9.
If you are participating casually while deliberately refusing repentance, remember the warning of 1 Corinthians 11.
If you have sinned against another person, do not use private prayer as an excuse to avoid appropriate confession, restitution, or reconciliation.
If you are trapped in repeated sin, seek the help, accountability, and pastoral care you need.

And if your conscience is constantly tormented by fears that you have forgotten some sin, remember that the sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice does not depend upon your ability to produce an exhaustive inventory of every failure.
Hebrews 10:14 declares:
“For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified.”
That verse does not mean Christians have already become morally flawless in daily conduct.
It points to the decisive sufficiency of Christ's sacrifice for those who belong to Him.
Our sanctification continues.
Our growth continues.
Our repentance continues.
But the foundation of our acceptance before God is Jesus Christ.
Not the quality of our memory.
Not the perfection of our confession.
Not the number of tears we shed.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
There is another important truth we should not overlook.
Christians from different church traditions do not all practice preparation for Communion in exactly the same way.
Roman Catholic teaching ordinarily requires sacramental confession before receiving Holy Communion when a person is conscious of grave sin, with particular provisions recognized by the Church.
Eastern Orthodox Christians commonly prepare through prayer, repentance, fasting, and confession according to their church's pastoral discipline.

Many Protestant churches emphasize personal examination, confession directly to God, repentance, faith, and reconciliation with others, while differing over who should receive Communion and how the elements are understood.
These differences are significant and should not be erased.
But the central biblical passages still demand our attention.
First Corinthians 11 commands self-examination and reverent participation.
First John 1:9 promises forgiveness and cleansing to those who confess their sins.
And the New Testament consistently places our hope in the saving work of Jesus Christ.
Therefore, Christians should approach Communion with honest repentance and reverence, while also respecting the biblical convictions and Communion discipline of their own church community.
The question is not whether confession matters.
It does.
The question is whether confession is a human achievement that earns Christ's grace.
It is not.
And now, before you move on, I want you to imagine something.
Imagine standing before the cross.
No congregation watching.
No religious reputation to protect.
No carefully chosen words to make yourself sound better.
Just you.
Your memories.
Your regrets.
The sins you confessed.
The sins you tried to excuse.
The people you hurt.
The things you have been afraid to bring into the light.
And before you stands the crucified Savior.
What would you say?
Would you begin explaining why you did what you did?
Would you compare yourself with someone who sinned more severely?
Would you remind Him of the good things you have accomplished?
Or would you finally say:
“Lord Jesus, have mercy on me. I have sinned. I cannot save myself. Thank You for dying for sinners. Teach me to turn from what dishonors You and to walk in Your truth.”
That is not weakness.
That is the beginning of spiritual honesty.
And spiritual honesty is far better than religious appearance.
The Lord's Table confronts the lie that we can save ourselves.
It also confronts the lie that we can embrace Christ while treating His commands as meaningless.
Grace is neither permission to remain enslaved to sin nor a reward for achieving perfection.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live godly lives.
The grace that forgives also teaches.
The Savior who receives repentant sinners also calls them to follow Him.
That is why repentance and faith belong together.
We do not turn from sin to prove we never needed a Savior.
We turn from sin because we have encountered the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you are reading this with a heavy heart, perhaps it is time to stop postponing the conversation you need to have with God.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you feel more spiritual.
Not when you have finally managed to repair your entire life.
You can begin with the truth right now.
Tell Him what you have done.
Tell Him what you are struggling with.
Ask Him for mercy.
Ask Him for strength to obey.
Where necessary, seek forgiveness from the people you have harmed.
And remember that repentance is not simply feeling terrible about yesterday.
It is turning toward Christ today.
The next time you hold the bread and cup, do not treat them casually.
Remember the body given for you.
Remember the blood shed for the forgiveness of sins.
Examine yourself.
Confess what needs confessing.
Turn from what needs turning from.
Seek reconciliation where it is needed.
And place your confidence not in your own worthiness but in the worthiness of Jesus Christ.
Because the Lord's Table is not a place to pretend you have never sinned. It is a place to remember the Savior whose death is our only hope of forgiveness.
If these words have uncovered something you have been hiding, do not bury that conviction beneath another ordinary Sunday.
Bring it before the Lord.
“Jesus, search my heart.”
Not as a public performance.
Not because commenting earns forgiveness.
But as a simple expression of your desire to walk honestly before Him.
If you are struggling and would appreciate prayer, you can also comment, “Pray for me.” You do not have to disclose private details or painful experiences publicly.
There may be someone reading the comments who has been fighting the same battle.
Someone who thought they were the only one.
Someone who needed to know that the call to repentance is also an invitation to receive the mercy of Christ.
And if God has restored you after a season of spiritual failure, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your story may encourage another person to stop running from the Lord and return to Him.
Do not underestimate what one honest testimony can mean to someone who is close to giving up.
There is also someone on your Facebook friends list who may be silently struggling with this very question.
Perhaps a believer who has avoided Communion for years because of shame.
Perhaps someone who receives it regularly without understanding Paul's warning.
Perhaps a family member who believes their past has permanently disqualified them from the mercy of Jesus.
Not simply to increase its reach, but to make biblical truth available to someone who may never ask the question aloud.
Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, those who have grown distant from church, those who are searching for truth, and even those who do not yet believe in Jesus to follow along.
Because the Gospel is not a private possession to be guarded from the people who need to hear it.
It is good news to be proclaimed.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, return to prayer, confront sin, or grow in your love for Christ, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to continuing and expanding the work of biblical teaching, Gospel-centered encouragement, and accessible discipleship resources.
These resources are intended to help people study Scripture, strengthen their faith, and continue learning beyond a single article or social media post.
And this work needs people who believe that sound biblical teaching should remain accessible.
For those who already practice giving to their local church, this may be an additional expression of generosity according to your circumstances and convictions.
And no payment can purchase God's favor, forgiveness, or spiritual blessing.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
That is the spirit in which this invitation is offered.
Freely.
Prayerfully.
Without pressure.
These are expressions of appreciation, not spiritual rewards or measures of anyone's faith.
The greatest gift we could ever point you toward is not something sold in a store.
It is the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
That is what matters most.
Because one day, the Communion elements we receive in remembrance will give way to the glorious reality toward which they point.
The Lord Jesus Christ will return.
And until that day, the church continues to proclaim His death.
The bread reminds us of His body.
The cup reminds us of His blood.
Our confession reminds us of our need.
And the Gospel reminds us of His sufficient grace.
So should Christians confess their sins before taking Communion?

Yes, believers should approach the Lord's Table with self-examination, sincere repentance, and honest confession before God, without imagining that they must become sinless or earn forgiveness before they may remember their Savior.
If you have been treating Communion lightly, take the warning seriously.
If you have been hiding from God, come into the light.
If you have been using grace as an excuse for disobedience, repent.
And if you have been convinced that your failures are stronger than the mercy of Christ, look again at the cross.
The risen Savior still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
He still forgives.
He still restores.
He still transforms.
And His finished work remains the only foundation upon which any of us can stand.
The bread in your hand does not proclaim that you have never fallen. It proclaims that Jesus Christ was broken for sinners—and that your fall does not have to be the final word of your story.
